name: GitHub
headline: Register in minutes with no review. The surprise comes later: each customer organization has to approve your app before it can see their org's data.

paths.name: OAuth app, personal repos
paths.note: No GitHub review at any point.

paths.name: Access to a customer's organization
paths.note: Wait depends on each customer's org owner approving the app.

prereqs.t: A GitHub account, or admin rights on the GitHub organization that should own the app.
A public homepage URL for your product.
The exact callback URL from your integration platform (in Composio, it is shown on the auth config).

steps.d: Sign in, then go to Settings, Developer settings, OAuth Apps. Register under your organization rather than a personal account so the app survives staff changes.
Application name and homepage are shown to users on the consent screen. Only use information you consider public; avoid internal URLs.
An OAuth app accepts a single authorization callback URL. Create separate apps for development and production instead of swapping the URL.
After registering, generate a client secret and copy it straight into your secrets manager or integration platform. It is shown once.
Paste the client ID and secret into your auth config. Only new connections use your app; existing users keep refreshing through the previous credentials until they reconnect.

nuances.d: OAuth apps need organization approval by default and cannot be approved per repository. A user in a restricted org can sign in, but org data stays hidden until an owner approves. Tell customers how to request access in your onboarding.

GitHub Apps allow up to 10 callback URLs and finer-grained permissions. If your platform supports GitHub Apps, compare before committing; this guide covers the OAuth app most integration platforms ask for.
Classic OAuth scopes such as repo grant broad access to private repositories. Users and security reviewers may push back; request the narrowest scope that works.

blockers.if: A user connects but sees none of their organization's repositories
blockers.then: The org has OAuth app access restrictions. The user requests access from the authorization screen and an org owner approves it in the org's settings.

blockers.if: You need different callback URLs per environment
blockers.then: Register one OAuth app per environment, or move to a GitHub App, which supports multiple callback URLs.

can: Draft the app name and description
Work out the callback URL from your integration platform
Open the exact registration page
Check the finished config against this guide
you: Sign in to GitHub (agents cannot pass the login wall)
Click Register and generate the secret
Store the secret safely
Ask customer org owners to approve the app

tested.what: Requested github.com/settings/applications/new and /settings/developers without an account
tested.result: Both return 302 to the GitHub sign-in page. The registration form cannot be reached unauthenticated, so field-level steps rely on GitHub's docs.

uncertain: How long customer org approval takes varies by customer; GitHub imposes no wait of its own.
Whether your integration platform supports GitHub Apps instead of OAuth apps.

name: Slack
headline: Creating the app takes under an hour. Selling it to other companies is the hard part: Slack's terms route commercial distribution through Marketplace review, and unlisted apps get a 1 request per minute limit on reading messages.

paths.name: Internal app for your own workspace
paths.note: Internal customer-built apps keep standard rate limits.

paths.name: Unlisted app installed by customers
paths.note: Works immediately, but message-history reads are throttled and the terms point commercial apps to the Marketplace.

paths.name: Slack Marketplace listing
paths.note: Needs 10 active workspace installs before you can submit. Slack publishes no review SLA.

prereqs.t: A Slack workspace where you can install apps, for testing.
An HTTPS redirect URL (your integration platform's callback).
For the Marketplace: at least 10 installations on active workspaces before you submit.

steps.t: Create the app from a manifest
steps.d: At api.slack.com/apps choose Create New App, then From a manifest. Paste the manifest below, which sets the name, redirect URL and scopes in one go.
Confirm the redirect URL and scopes under OAuth & Permissions. Ask only for scopes you use; reviewers check this.

steps.t: Install to your own workspace and test
steps.d: Install, complete a real OAuth connection through your integration, and call one API method.
Under Manage Distribution, work through Slack's checklist and activate public distribution so other workspaces can install the app.
If you charge customers and read message history, plan the Marketplace submission early. You need 10 active installs first, so recruit design partners.

snippet.label: App manifest your agent can generate
snippet.code:
display_information:
  name: Acme Agent
oauth_config:
  redirect_urls:
    - https://YOUR-CALLBACK-URL
  scopes:
    bot:
      - channels:read
      - chat:write
settings:
  org_deploy_enabled: false
  socket_mode_enabled: false

nuances.t: Reading history is throttled for unlisted apps
nuances.d: For commercially distributed apps outside the Marketplace, conversations.history and conversations.replies are limited to 1 request per minute, with the page size cut to 15 objects. This hit new apps from May 29, 2025 and existing installs from March 3, 2026. An agent that summarizes channels will feel this immediately.

nuances.t: The terms point commercial apps to the Marketplace
nuances.d: Slack's updated API terms say the Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercially distributing apps, including unlisted ones.
Apps a customer builds for their own workspace keep their existing rate limits.
If you are reusing an old classic app, Slack's deprecation date is November 16, 2026. Create a new app instead.

blockers.if: Your agent returns only 15 messages and hits 429 errors
blockers.then: You are on the non-Marketplace limit. Cache aggressively, backfill slowly using the Retry-After header, and start the Marketplace path.

blockers.if: You cannot reach 10 active installs for the Marketplace
blockers.then: Ship as unlisted to design partners first, within the rate limits, and submit once you have the installs.

can: Generate the app manifest with the right scopes and redirect URL
Pick the minimum scopes from your feature list
Draft Marketplace listing copy and scope justifications
Flag API calls that the rate limit will affect
you: Sign in and create the app
Install it to a workspace and test
Activate distribution
Recruit the first 10 installs and submit to the Marketplace

tested.result: Not reachable from the sandbox (network allowlist). Setup steps rely on Slack's docs and are marked accordingly.

uncertain: Marketplace review time. Slack does not publish one; the range shown is a planning estimate, not a sourced figure.
Slack's changelog says the 10-install entry requirement is changing. Check the current Marketplace guidelines before you plan around it.
Exact wording of the Manage Distribution checklist (not verified first-hand).

name: Gmail (Google)
headline: The OAuth client takes 20 minutes. Reading email is the longest path in this library: Google verification plus an annual third-party security assessment, usually weeks and not free.

paths.name: Testing mode (up to 100 test users)
paths.note: Refresh tokens expire after 7 days. Fine for demos, breaks production sync.

paths.name: Send only (gmail.send, a sensitive scope)
paths.note: Verification and a demo video, but no security assessment.

paths.name: Read or modify mail (restricted scopes)
paths.note: Verification plus a CASA security assessment, renewed every year.

prereqs.t: A Google Cloud project with the Gmail API enabled.
A public homepage and privacy policy on a domain you own.
A demo video showing how you use each sensitive or restricted scope.
For restricted scopes: your product must fit one of Google's permitted Gmail application types.
For restricted scopes: budget for a CASA assessment from a Google-approved lab.

steps.d: This decides the whole timeline. Every Gmail read scope, including gmail.readonly, is restricted. gmail.send is only sensitive. If your agent only sends mail, stop at gmail.send.

steps.t: Create the project and enable the Gmail API
steps.d: In Google Cloud console, create a project for production (separate from dev) and enable the Gmail API.
Set the app name, logo, support email, homepage and privacy policy. Choose External unless only your own Workspace users will connect.
Create a Web application client and add your integration platform's redirect URI exactly.

steps.t: Test with up to 100 test users
steps.d: Add test users and run real connections. Expect refresh tokens to expire after 7 days in this mode.
Submit scope justifications and the demo video. For restricted scopes, start the CASA assessment with an approved lab in parallel.
Restricted-scope verification and CASA must be renewed every year. Put the date on a calendar.

nuances.t: Testing mode breaks after a week
nuances.d: External apps in Testing get refresh tokens that expire after 7 days, so a connection that works on Monday stops syncing the next week.
Until verified, only 100 users can ever authorize the app. Spend them on real testers, not on your team's repeated logins.
When a user changes their Google password, refresh tokens with Gmail scopes are invalidated. Build a reconnect prompt.
If only users in your own Google Workspace organization connect, an Internal app avoids verification entirely.
Drafting is restricted even though sending is not. Scope names are a poor guide to risk tier; check Google's list.

blockers.then: The user is not on the test user list, or you requested a restricted scope that is not yet verified.

blockers.if: Verification asks for changes to your privacy policy
blockers.then: Google expects the policy to describe exactly how Gmail data is used, stored and shared. Your agent can draft the section; legal should approve it.
Fix and rescan. Running a static scan before engaging a lab avoids most first-round failures.

can: Map your features to the narrowest scope set and its tier
Draft scope justifications and the privacy policy section on Gmail data
Write a script and shot list for the demo video
Pre-check your app with a static security scan before CASA
you: Create the project and OAuth client in Google Cloud
Verify domain ownership
Record the demo video
Pay for and complete the CASA assessment
Submit and answer reviewer emails

tested.what: Attempted to reach console.cloud.google.com from the agent environment
tested.result: Not reachable from the sandbox. Guidance draws on Google support pages and integration-vendor runbooks (Nango, Nylas, Unified), labeled per claim.

uncertain: Total wait. Nango reports CASA Tier 2 can finish in about 5 days and suggests budgeting 10 to 20; Google says it can take several weeks or longer. The range shown spans both.
CASA cost varies by lab and tier; no reliable figure was found.
Wait for sensitive-only verification is an estimate, not a sourced figure.

name: LinkedIn
headline: Sign-in and posting as a member are instant checkboxes. Anything involving company pages is a separate product, a separate app, and a review queue.

paths.name: Sign in and post as the member
paths.note: OpenID Connect plus Share on LinkedIn, granted instantly.

paths.name: Manage company pages (Community Management API)
paths.note: Development tier, then Standard tier with a screencast. Needs its own app.

prereqs.t: A LinkedIn Company Page you administer. Every app must be associated with one.
The page admin available to approve the verification link.
An app logo and your redirect URL.

steps.d: At linkedin.com/developers/apps, create an app, associate your Company Page, upload a logo and accept the terms.
Generate the verification URL in app settings and have a page admin open it. The app does nothing until it shows Verified.
On the Products tab, add Sign In with LinkedIn using OpenID Connect (openid, profile, email) and Share on LinkedIn (w_member_social).

steps.t: Add the redirect URL and copy credentials
steps.d: On the Auth tab, add your platform's redirect URL and copy the client ID and secret into your auth config.

steps.t: For company pages, create a second app
steps.d: Community Management API cannot share an app with other products. Create a dedicated app and apply; expect a Development tier first and a Standard tier review with a screencast.

nuances.t: Company page features need a separate app
nuances.d: If you add Community Management API to the same app as sign-in, you will have to split them. Plan two apps from the start.
LinkedIn gates several products on a verified Company Page. Attach your real company page, not a throwaway.

nuances.t: Sign In with LinkedIn is not identity verification
nuances.d: It proves account control, not that the person is who their profile says.

blockers.then: The page association has not been approved. Send the verification URL to a page admin.

blockers.if: You get unauthorized_scope_error for organization scopes
blockers.then: Those need Community Management API on a dedicated app, approved through review.

can: Tell you which products your features need, and whether you need one app or two
Draft the Community Management API application and screencast script
Check that requested scopes match the added products
you: Create the app while signed in
Get a page admin to approve verification
Submit the Community Management API application

tested.what: Attempted to reach linkedin.com/developers/apps from the agent environment
tested.result: Not reachable from the sandbox. A third-party developer reported completing the self-serve path end to end in about 15 minutes in 2026.

LinkedIn's official Learn docs were not fetched directly in this check; most step details come from integration vendors' setup guides.

name: Salesforce
headline: Most tutorials online are now wrong. New Connected Apps are disabled by default since Spring '26, and customer orgs block uninstalled apps, so plan for an External Client App that each customer's admin installs.

paths.name: External Client App in your own org
paths.note: Works for your org. Reaching customer orgs needs more (below).

paths.name: Customers connect their own orgs
paths.note: Package the app and have each customer admin install it.

prereqs.t: A Salesforce org you control, such as a free Developer Edition org.
Admin access in that org.
To reach customer orgs: a packaging setup (second-generation packaging) and customer admins willing to install.

steps.t: Create an External Client App, not a Connected App
steps.d: From Setup, open External Client App Manager and create a new app. Connected App creation is disabled by default and needs Salesforce Support to re-enable.

steps.t: Enable OAuth and set the callback
steps.d: Enable OAuth, add your platform's callback URL and select scopes (typically api and refresh_token).

steps.t: Copy the consumer key and secret
steps.d: Paste them into your auth config. Use the web server flow; External Client Apps do not support the username-password flow.
Add the app to a second-generation package so customer orgs can install it, and give customers install instructions.

steps.t: Have each customer admin install it
steps.d: Since September 2025, users are blocked from authorizing uninstalled connected apps unless an admin installs the app or grants a bypass permission.

nuances.d: Creation of new Connected Apps is restricted as of Spring '26. Existing ones keep working; new integrations should use External Client Apps.

nuances.t: Uninstalled apps are blocked for new users
nuances.d: New users cannot authorize an uninstalled connected app unless they hold Approve Uninstalled Connected Apps or Use Any API Client. Expect support tickets from customers who skip the install step.
External Client Apps drop the username-password OAuth flow some older scripts relied on.
Local External Client Apps are not copied when a sandbox is cloned or refreshed; only packaged ones are.

blockers.if: There is no New Connected App button
blockers.then: Expected since Spring '26. Use External Client App Manager, or ask Salesforce Support to re-enable Connected Apps if you truly need one.

blockers.if: Customer users get blocked when connecting
blockers.then: Their admin must install the app (Setup, Connected Apps OAuth Usage, Install) or grant the bypass permission to specific users.

can: Spot outdated Connected App instructions in your docs
Draft the customer admin install guide
Generate packaging metadata for the app
Pick the right OAuth flow for your use case
you: Create the org and the External Client App
Set up packaging and a Dev Hub
Coordinate installs with each customer admin

tested.what: Attempted to reach Salesforce setup pages from the agent environment
tested.result: Not reachable from the sandbox. Guidance draws on Salesforce developer docs and vendor migration notes.

uncertain: Whether an unpackaged External Client App can serve users in other orgs. Vendor notes imply packaging is required; Salesforce's own wording was not confirmed directly.
AppExchange security review timing, if you choose to list. Not researched in this pass.

name: X (Twitter)
headline: No review queue, but no free lunch: since February 2026 every new developer pays per request, and X's terms point commercial products to an Enterprise contract.

paths.name: Pay-per-use app
paths.note: Buy credits before your first call. Reads capped at 2 million posts a month.

paths.name: Commercial product at scale
paths.note: Enterprise plan, negotiated with X sales.

prereqs.t: An X developer account, with a description of your use case.
A payment method and prepaid credits.
Your callback URL and a website URL.

steps.d: Sign up at developer.x.com and describe your use case. New accounts start on pay-per-use.
In the Developer Console, create the app that will hold your OAuth credentials.
In user authentication settings, enable OAuth 2.0 as a web app (confidential client), and add the callback and website URLs.
Typical agent scopes are tweet.read, users.read and tweet.write; add offline.access to get refresh tokens.

steps.t: Buy credits and set a spend limit
steps.d: Load credits in the Developer Console and set limits before connecting users, so a runaway loop drains a capped balance rather than your card.

nuances.t: The free tier is gone for new developers
nuances.d: On February 6, 2026, X made pay-per-use the default for new developers. Price varies by endpoint; check the Developer Console for current rates.

nuances.t: Self-serve is meant for limited use
nuances.d: Per an Open Terms Archive memo on X's developer terms, self-serve use targets prototypes and apps with a limited number of end users; commercial use still requires the Enterprise plan. Read the current terms before launching to customers.
Pay-per-use reads are capped at 2 million posts per month before Enterprise is needed.

nuances.t: Every user's agent actions cost you
nuances.d: Each call your users' agents make spends your credits. Model per-user cost before pricing your product.

blockers.if: Calls fail with a payment or credits error
blockers.then: Your balance is empty. Top up, and turn on auto-recharge with a cap.

blockers.if: Your product is commercial with many end users
blockers.then: Contact X about Enterprise before launch; plan the timeline around a sales conversation.

can: Estimate monthly API cost from your expected usage
Pick scopes and the OAuth 2.0 client type
Draft the use case description
Summarize current developer terms for your use case
you: Create the developer account and app
Add payment and set spend limits
Decide whether you need Enterprise, and talk to X

tested.what: Attempted to reach developer.x.com from the agent environment
tested.result: Not reachable from the sandbox. No official X page was fetched in this check; claims are from secondary reports and labeled so.

uncertain: Exact per-request prices. Third-party reports cite about $0.01 per post created and $0.005 per post read; X shows current prices in the console.

Enterprise timeline and cost; not publicly documented.
